# Overview

This report completes the exercises for **STAT3102/6102 Week 3 SGTA**, focusing on categorical visualization techniques (pie charts, standard bar charts, and Pareto charts) and continuous distribution analysis (histograms, bin width exploration, and comparative boxplots).

---

# Exercise 1: Categorical Data Visualisations (`stat270.csv`)

Recall that the dataset `stat270.csv` contains three variables: `ID`, `Country`, and `Statdiv` (Statistical Division). Here, we construct pie charts, ordered bar charts, and Pareto charts for the `Statdiv` variable.

```{r ex1-data}
# Read stat270 dataset
stat270 <- read_csv("stat270.csv")

# Standardise column names to lowercase so Statdiv becomes statdiv
colnames(stat270) <- tolower(colnames(stat270))

# Clean and summarise statistical division counts
df_statdiv <- stat270 %>%
  filter(!is.na(statdiv)) %>%
  count(statdiv, name = "counts") %>%
  mutate(percentage = round(counts / sum(counts) * 100, 1))
```

### 1. Pie Chart
While pie charts rely on angle and area perception, adding direct labels improves clarity.

```{r ex1-pie}
ggplot(df_statdiv, aes(x = "", y = counts, fill = statdiv)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Students by Statistical Division",
    subtitle = "Pie Chart Display",
    fill = "Statistical Division"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))
```

### 2. Standard & Ordered Bar Chart (Pareto Chart)
Ordering the categories by frequency creates a **Pareto Chart**, applying Cleveland's principle of position along a common scale and adhering to Wainer's rule against arbitrary orderings.

```{r ex1-pareto}
ggplot(df_statdiv, aes(x = reorder(statdiv, -counts), y = counts, fill = statdiv)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = counts), vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Pareto Chart: Student Counts by Statistical Division",
    x = "Statistical Division",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
  )
```

# Exercise 2: Australian Prison Population Analysis (ABS 2024)

This exercise analyses prisoner data by most serious offence/charge and legal status (sentenced vs. unsentenced) across sexes, sourced from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS 2024).

```{r ex2-data}
# Construct prisoners tibble as specified
prisoners <- tibble(
  Offence = c(
    "Homicide", "Acts to Cause Injury", "Sexual Assault", "Dangerous/Negligent Acts",
    "Abduction/Harassment", "Robbery/Extortion", "Unlawful Entry", "Theft",
    "Fraud/Deception", "Illicit Drugs", "Weapons/Explosives", "Property Damage",
    "Public Order", "Traffic/Vehicle", "Offences Against Justice", "Miscellaneous"
  ),
  total_males = c(3061, 11335, 7244, 1413, 610, 2332, 3434, 1302, 437, 4663, 826, 558, 138, 338, 3104, 71),
  total_females = c(298, 980, 111, 119, 45, 239, 327, 225, 127, 550, 46, 70, 11, 36, 239, 10)
)

# Reshape data to long format for side-by-side ggplot visualisations
prisoners_long <- prisoners %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(total_males, total_females),
    names_to = "Sex",
    names_prefix = "total_",
    values_to = "Count"
  ) %>%
  mutate(Sex = ifelse(Sex == "males", "Males", "Females"))
```

### Side-by-Side Comparative Bar Chart
Comparing total male and female prisoner counts across major offence types:

```{r ex2-barchart}
ggplot(prisoners_long, aes(x = Offence, y = Count, fill = Sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Males" = "#2b5c8f", "Females" = "#d95f02")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Australian Prisoner Population by Offence & Sex (ABS 2024)",
    x = "Most Serious Offence / Charge",
    y = "Number of Prisoners",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)
  )
```

### Comparative Pareto Chart (Ordered by Offence Volume)
Sorting offences by total volume facilitates clearer visual evaluation of high-frequency offences.

```{r ex2-pareto}
# Sort offences by combined total
prisoners_long <- prisoners_long %>%
  group_by(Offence) %>%
  mutate(Total_Offence = sum(Count)) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(prisoners_long, aes(x = reorder(Offence, -Total_Offence), y = Count, fill = Sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Males" = "#1f78b4", "Females" = "#e31a1c")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Pareto Chart: Prisoner Offence Categories Ordered by Frequency",
    x = "Offence Category",
    y = "Number of Prisoners",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)
  )
```

# Exercise 3: School Suspension Analysis (`truant.csv`)

This section explores school suspension data from NSW districts (1998) to evaluate the impact of bin width, starting points, and boxplots on statistical communication.

```{r ex3-data}
truant <- read_csv("truant.csv")

# Convert gender to labelled factor (1 = Male, 2 = Female)
truant <- truant %>%
  mutate(Gender = factor(gender, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female")))
```

### Descriptive Statistics: Total Long Suspensions

```{r ex3-summary}
summary_stats <- truant %>%
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(long, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(long, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median = median(long, na.rm = TRUE),
    IQR = IQR(long, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min = min(long, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max = max(long, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

kable(summary_stats, digits = 2, caption = "Summary Statistics: Long Suspensions")
```

### Bin Width & Histogram Parameter Exploration

Comparing default bin widths against widths of 40 and 20:

```{r ex3-histograms, fig.height=8}
p1 <- ggplot(truant, aes(x = long)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#3182bd", color = "white") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Default R Bin Width", x = "Long Suspensions", y = "Count")

p2 <- ggplot(truant, aes(x = long)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 40, fill = "#3182bd", color = "white") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Bin Width = 40", x = "Long Suspensions", y = "Count")

p3 <- ggplot(truant, aes(x = long)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 20, fill = "#3182bd", color = "white") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Bin Width = 20", x = "Long Suspensions", y = "Count")

library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 1)
```

**Analytical Observations:**
* **Effect of Bin Width = 40:** Over-smooths the distribution, hiding localized peaks and right-skew detail.
* **Effect of Bin Width = 20:** Strikes a strong balance between noise reduction and structural clarity, clearly capturing the right-skewed distribution of suspensions across school districts.

### Comparative Boxplots: Males vs. Females

```{r ex3-boxplots}
ggplot(truant, aes(x = Gender, y = long, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.color = "red") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Male" = "#2c7fb8", "Female" = "#fa9fb5")) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparative Boxplot: Long Suspensions by Gender",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Number of Long Suspensions"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13))
```

# Integration with Lecture Principles

* **Cleveland & McGill Hierarchy:** Ordering categories in Exercises 1 and 2 onto a **position along a common scale** significantly outperforms pie chart angle evaluation[cite: 43, 53].
* **Wainer's Rules:** Avoided "Alabama First" (arbitrary sorting) by implementing Pareto reordering[cite: 36, 53].
* **Data-to-Ink Ratio:** Minimalist themes (`theme_minimal()`) and precise bin selections preserve data density without chartjunk[cite: 11, 15, 53].
